lead: On the Sixth Sunday of Easter one word runs through all three readings: love. In the house of Cornelius, Peter learns that God shows no partiality, and the Holy Spirit falls on Gentiles before anyone has baptised them. John’s letter gives the shortest description of God in the Bible: God is love. In the Gospel Jesus shows how far that love goes: to laying down one’s life for one’s friends.

The order matters. Love begins with God, not with us (1 John 4:10). It flows from the Father to the Son, from the Son to the disciples (John 15:9), and from them outward, even to a Roman officer’s household in Caesarea. Psalm 98 sings that the Lord has made known his victory in the sight of the nations; Acts shows it happening.

set: Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously and prayed constantly (10:1–2). An angel told him to send for Peter at Joppa. Meanwhile Peter, praying on a rooftop, saw a sheet let down from heaven full of creatures the Law counted unclean, and heard a voice telling him not to call profane what God has made clean (10:15). Then the messengers of Cornelius arrived at the door.

Background. Jewish law and custom kept a careful separation from Gentile homes and tables, as Peter himself says (10:28). It was meant to guard Israel’s holiness as God’s own people. Now Peter learns that God is also calling the Gentiles. The reading leaves out Peter’s summary of the Gospel (vv. 36–43), one of the great sermons of Acts, and moves to the moment when the Spirit interrupts him.
str: vv. 25–26: Cornelius falls at Peter’s feet; Peter raises him up.
vv. 44–46: the Spirit falls on the Gentiles, and they speak in tongues and praise God.
vv. 47–48: Peter orders them to be baptised.

¶ Luke tells this story three times: in full in chapter 10, again in Peter’s report (11:1–18), and briefly at the meeting in Jerusalem (15:7–9). Repetition is his way of saying: this is a turning point.
kw: Literally one who “receives the face”, who judges by appearance, rank or race (v. 34). The Old Testament already says that God is not partial (Deuteronomy 10:17). Peter now sees what this means for the nations.
“The gift of the Holy Spirit” (v. 45) is the same phrase Peter used at Pentecost (2:38). The Gentiles receive the very same gift, not a lesser one, as Peter later insists (11:17).

The verb of Joel’s prophecy quoted at Pentecost: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (2:17). Here “all flesh” begins to include the Gentiles. The scene is often called the Pentecost of the Gentiles.
vv: But Peter made him get up, saying, “Stand up; I am only a mortal.”
Cornelius meant deep reverence, but Peter will not accept what belongs to God alone. The first of the apostles begins by lifting a man to his feet.
I truly understand that God shows no partiality,
Peter speaks as one still learning. Even the first of the apostles had to be taught by the Spirit, through a vision and through the faith of a Gentile.
but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

This does not mean that Christ is unnecessary: Peter at once goes on to preach Christ, and the passage ends in baptism. It means that God was already at work in Cornelius before Peter arrived, preparing him for the Gospel.
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word.
God does not wait for Peter to finish. Elsewhere in Acts the Spirit comes with or after baptism (2:38; 8:14–17). Here he comes first, so that no one can doubt that God has accepted these Gentiles.
“Can anyone withhold the water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?”
The Spirit’s coming does not make baptism unnecessary; it is the reason Peter cannot refuse it. The gift within is joined to the sacrament of the Church.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its chapter on the People of God with v. 35: at all times and in every nation, anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him; yet God willed to make people holy and to save them not as individuals without any bond between them, but by making them into a single people (Lumen Gentium 9, in substance). That is the whole movement of this chapter of Acts: God at work in Cornelius, and then Cornelius brought into the one Church through baptism. The Council also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will, can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16).

set: John has just told his readers to test the spirits, because not every spirit is from God (4:1–6). Now he turns to the sign that does not deceive: love. This passage is the heart of the letter, and the words “God is love” return a few verses later (4:16).

Ancient tradition ascribes the letter to the apostle John. The letter does not name its writer, and many scholars think it comes from a disciple within the circle of John. It was written for communities wounded by division, near the end of the first century.
str: v. 7: let us love one another, because love is from God.
v. 8: whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.
v. 9: how God’s love was revealed: he sent his only Son.
v. 10: what love is: not our love for God, but his love for us.
kw: A word rare in earlier Greek writing, which the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament made their own for the love that gives itself. In English, “love”, “loves” and “loved” occur nine times in these four verses.
God sent “his only Son” (v. 9). The word means the one and only of his kind. John uses it of the Son in his Gospel too (1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). The gift is measured by what it cost.

The means by which sin is taken away and communion with God restored (v. 10; also 2:2). It recalls the Day of Atonement. John does not picture an angry God being won over: it is God who loves first and who himself sends the Son.
vv: Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God;
John does not first say “love, because it is commanded”, but “love, because love comes from God”. To love is to let God’s own life pass through us.
Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.

Knowing God here is not having information about him but sharing his life. John does not say that love is God; he says that God is love. The one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is in his very being love.
God sent his only Son into the world so that we might live through him.
Love is revealed not in a feeling but in a sending, and the purpose is life.
In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us
Every Christian life begins by being loved. We do not earn God’s love by our love; our love is the answer to his.
ch: Pope Benedict XVI began his first encyclical, Deus Caritas Est (2005), with 1 John 4:16, which repeats today’s v. 8, and said that these words express with remarkable clarity the heart of the Christian faith (in substance). The Catechism teaches that in saying “God is love” John affirms that God’s very being is love, and that by sending his Son and the Spirit, God has revealed his innermost secret: he himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (CCC 221). It quotes v. 10 to show that the Father’s giving up of his Son for our sins comes from love that goes before any merit of ours (CCC 604).

set: The Last Supper, just after the image of the vine and the branches (15:1–8). Jesus now says plainly what the sap of the vine is: his love, which he has received from the Father. The passage moves from love received (v. 9), to love kept (v. 10), to love given away (vv. 12–13), and ends where it began, with the command to love (v. 17).
He speaks on the night before he dies. When he says that no one has greater love than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends (v. 13), he is describing what he will do the next day.
str: v. 9: as the Father has loved me; abide in my love.
vv. 10–11: keeping the commandments, and joy made complete.
vv. 12–13: love one another as I have loved you; the greatest love.
vv. 14–15: no longer servants but friends.
vv. 16–17: chosen and appointed to bear fruit that will last; love one another.
kw: Not an equal in power, but one with whom a person shares his heart (v. 15). In the Old Testament Abraham is called God’s friend (Isaiah 41:8; see James 2:23), and the Lord spoke with Moses as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11). What was given to a few is now given to all the disciples.
To remain, to make one’s home (vv. 9–10). Love here is not a passing moment but a dwelling place.
Joy is the purpose of his words (v. 11). It is his own joy, which does not depend on circumstances, and which, in the same discourse, he says no one will take from them (16:22).
vv: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
The love the disciples receive is the same love that flows between the Father and the Son. Nothing less is offered.
This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
The “as” is both the measure and the source. We cannot love as he did by our own strength; we can love because he has first loved us.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
St Paul goes further still: Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). The friends for whom Jesus dies include those who will deny and abandon him that very night.
I do not call you servants any longer,

Being a servant of God is no disgrace; Paul proudly calls himself a servant of Christ Jesus (Romans 1:1). But a servant is told what to do, while a friend is told why. Jesus has shared with them all that he has heard from the Father.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Usually a disciple chose his teacher. Here the Teacher chooses. A vocation begins with being chosen, and so it rests more on his faithfulness than on ours.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 9 and 12 when it teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment: by loving one another the disciples imitate the love of Jesus which they themselves receive (CCC 1823). St Thomas Aquinas, appealing to v. 15, teaches that charity is a friendship of man with God (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 23, a. 1, in substance). The Church sees the fullest form of v. 13 in the martyrs, and also in every hidden life spent for others.

qa: Does “God shows no partiality” mean that all religions are the same?

No. Peter says it and then preaches Christ and baptises. The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions and sees in them, often, a ray of the Truth that enlightens all people; at the same time she proclaims Christ, the way, the truth and the life, in whom people find the fullness of religious life (Nostra Aetate 2). God’s welcome to every nation is the reason for the mission, not a reason to give it up.
If “God is love”, how can there be judgment?

Love is not indifference. A love that did not care whether we lived or destroyed ourselves would not be love. The same passage says that God sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10): God takes sin seriously because he loves. The Church teaches that only one who finally and of his own will refuses that merciful love remains separated from him (CCC 1033).
Jesus says “I chose you”. Did he not choose everyone?

At the Supper he speaks first to the Twelve, whom he chose and appointed to go and bear fruit. But every Christian is chosen in Christ (Ephesians 1:4), and the call is offered to all. To be chosen is not a privilege to keep for oneself, but a sending: “to go and bear fruit”.
rite: In India the Solemnity of the Ascension is kept next Sunday, 9 May. The days between the Ascension and Pentecost recall the apostles devoted to prayer together with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14), the prayer from which the Pentecost novena takes its pattern. Peter’s question about the water of baptism makes this a good Sunday for the rite of blessing and sprinkling of water, which the Roman Missal allows in place of the penitential act on Sundays, especially in Easter Time. On Thursday and Friday of last week the weekday Mass read the two halves of today’s Gospel (John 15:9–11 and 15:12–17); today they are heard together, with John’s letter as their commentary.
study: Where have I seen God at work in someone before they knew him, as he was in Cornelius?
John says that love begins with God’s love for us. When did I last simply let myself be loved by God, in prayer or in confession?
Jesus calls me his friend, not his servant. How would my prayer change if I spoke to him as a friend?
For whom am I being asked to lay down a little of my life this week: my time, my pride, my comfort?
